claim: Interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM) occurs in synchrony with the cell cycle in pseudostratified epithelia.
source: More than 80 years ago, these movements, termed interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM), were shown to occur in synchrony with their cell cycle (Sauer, 1935).

claim: Nuclei of proliferating cells undergo mitosis exclusively at the apical surface under normal conditions.
source: Under normal conditions, nuclei of proliferating cells undergo mitosis (M) exclusively at the apical surface.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: During G1 phase, nuclei migrate away from the apical surface to reach more basal positions by S phase.
source: During the first gap phase (G1) of the cell cycle, nuclei migrate away from this surface to reach more basal positions by synthesis phase (S), when DNA is replicated.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: In G2 phase, nuclei migrate rapidly toward the apical surface where they divide again.
source: In the second gap phase (G2), nuclei migrate rapidly toward the apical surface where they divide again (Del Bene, 2011; Sauer, 1935; Baye and Link, 2007; Leung et al., 2011; Kosodo et al., 2011; Norden et al., 2009).

claim: In the zebrafish retina, the actomyosin complex alone moves nuclei to the apical surface during G2.
source: while in the zebrafish retina, it appears to be the actomyosin complex alone that moves the nuclei to the apical surface during G2 (Norden et al., 2009; Leung et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Norden et al., 2009 and Leung et al., 2011

claim: IKNM affects morphogenesis and cell differentiation in neural tissues.
source: Importantly, IKNM is known to affect morphogenesis and cell differentiation in neural tissues (Spear and Erickson, 2012), as retinas with perturbed IKNM are known to develop prematurely and to display abnormalities in cell composition (Del Bene et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Spear and Erickson, 2012 and Del Bene et al., 2008

claim: Nuclear movement during G1 and S phases resembles a stochastic process with mean squared displacements growing linearly in time.
source: On a phenomenological level, studies tracking individual nuclei in the zebrafish retina during the G1 and S phases have shown their movement to resemble a stochastic process (Norden et al., 2009; Leung et al., 2011), particularly in the form of the mean squared nuclear displacement versus time.
evidence: Supported by citations to Norden et al., 2009 and Leung et al., 2011

claim: Individual nuclei switch between apical and basal movements at random intervals during G1 and S phases.
source: During these periods, individual nuclei switch between apical and basal movements at random intervals, leading to great variability in the maximum basal position they reach during each cell cycle (Baye and Link, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baye and Link, 2007

claim: There is a slow basalward drift of the entire population of nuclei during IKNM.
source: In addition to the stochastic movements of nuclei during IKNM, there is also a slow basalward drift of the entire population of nuclei.
evidence: Stated as an observation in the field

claim: Nuclear-sized microbeads inserted between cells during IKNM in the mouse cortex exhibit variable basalward-biased migration.
source: As variable basalward-biased migration was observed in nuclear-sized microbeads inserted in between cells during IKNM in the mouse cortex (Kosodo et al., 2011), it seems likely that passive forces are involved in this drift.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kosodo et al., 2011

claim: Retinas were imaged at 2 min intervals for optimal temporal resolution.
source: We imaged fluorescently labeled nuclei of whole retinas of developing zebrafish at 2 min intervals, an optimal time period given the difficulty to track nuclei accurately over long times and the increased photobleaching with shorter intervals.

claim: Comparing movies at 2 min and 20 s intervals over 2 hrs showed no difference in analyses.
source: We compared movies of retinas imaged at 2 min and at 20 s intervals over a period of 2 hrs and found that the improvement in temporal resolution made no difference to our analyses.

claim: H2B-GFP transgenic lines were used with GFP expression exclusively in the nuclei.
source: To follow the nuclei of all cells within a portion of the retina, we used H2B-GFP transgenic lines with GFP expression exclusively in the nuclei (Figure 1A).
evidence: Described as experimental method and shown in Figure 1A

claim: Both lightsheet and two-photon microscopy produce images with minimal bleaching compared to other microscopic techniques.
source: Both of these methods yield images with minimal bleaching compared to other microscopic techniques (Svoboda and Yasuda, 2006; Stelzer, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Svoboda and Yasuda, 2006 and Stelzer, 2015

claim: Automated tracking yielded an average linkage accuracy of approximately 65%.
source: The most optimal combination of parameters yielded an average linkage accuracy, from each time point to the next, of approximately 65%.

claim: Most daughter nuclei move away from the apical surface within minutes of being born with a clear basalward bias.
source: Most daughter nuclei move away from the apical surface, within minutes of being born, with a clear basalward bias in their speed distribution (Figure 2C).
evidence: Described as experimental observation and shown in Figure 2C

claim: After the brief basal movement period, nuclear speeds become equally distributed between basalward and apicalward with a mean near 0.
source: However, immediately after this brief period, nuclear speeds become much more equally distributed between basalward and apicalward, with a mean value near 0.

claim: An apical clearing of a few microns exists for dividing cells except during mitosis.
source: Interestingly, except during mitosis, we find an apical clearing of a few microns for dividing cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: Described as experimental observation and shown in Figure 2D

claim: The average length of the nuclear long axis right before division (5.0 ± 0.7 µm) is not significantly different from other times in the cell cycle (5.3 ± 1.1 µm).
source: We found no significant difference between the average length of the nuclear long axis when measured for 50 random nuclei right before their division (5.0 ± 0.7 µm) compared to 50 others chosen randomly from any other time point within the cell cycle (5.3 ± 1.1 µm), indicating that this clearing is likely to have a biological explanation, such as the preferential occupancy of M phase nuclei and surrounding cytoplasm at the apical surface during IKNM.

claim: Nuclear long axis length is significantly decreased 10 min after division (3.9 ± 0.5 µm) compared to M phase.
source: We also performed the same measurements for 25 random nuclei 10 min after division when the average long axis length is significantly decreased by 0.8 fold (3.9 ± 0.5 µm).

claim: Nuclear long axis length increases significantly in the 10 min following the initial post-division decrease (4.8 ± 0.7 µm).
source: However, this measurement increased significantly in the following 10 min (4.8 ± 0.7 µm) to become similar to that at M phase.

claim: When RPCs are pharmacologically inhibited from replicating DNA, their nuclei neither enter G2 nor exhibit rapid persistent apical migration.
source: Previous work has shown that when RPCs are pharmacologically inhibited from replicating their DNA, their nuclei neither enter G2 nor exhibit rapid persistent apical migration that normally occurs during the G2 phase of the cell cycle (Leung et al., 2011; Kosodo et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Leung et al., 2011 and Kosodo et al., 2011

claim: Stochastic movements of nuclei in G1 and S phases slow down considerably when DNA replication is inhibited.
source: A more surprising result of these experiments is that the stochastic movements of nuclei in G1 and S phases also slow down considerably during such treatment (Leung et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leung et al., 2011

claim: There is no correlation between the speed of movement of nuclei and the average speed of their neighbors.
source: Figure 3A shows the lack of correlation between the speed of movement of nuclei and the average speed of their neighbors.
evidence: Described as experimental result and shown in Figure 3A

claim: No correlation was found between speeds of neighboring nuclei categorized by position, direction, or time delay.
source: We further categorized the neighboring nuclei by their position in relation to the nucleus of interest (along the apicobasal axis), their direction of movement, and whether they were moving in the same direction of the nucleus of interest or not. None of the resulting eight categories of neighboring nuclei showed a correlation in their average speed with the speed of the nucleus of interest.

claim: There does not appear to be much transfer of kinetic energy between neighboring nuclei.
source: These results suggest that there does not appear to be much transfer of kinetic energy between neighboring nuclei, and this is consistent with general considerations of the strongly overdamped character of motion at these length scales.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results and physical considerations

claim: A nuclear concentration gradient is generated because nuclei divide exclusively at the apical surface.
source: In diffusion, a concentration gradient drives the average movement of particles from areas of high to areas of low concentration. However, despite the average movement being directed, each individual particle's trajectory is a random walk (Reif, 1965). Similarly, during IKNM a gradient in nuclear concentration is generated because nuclei divide exclusively at the apical surface.
evidence: Inferred from biological observation and comparison to diffusion

claim: In HU-AC-treated retinas, the mean of the nuclear distribution moved further toward the basal surface over 160 min.
source: As expected from the diffusion model (Figure 4D), over the course of 160 min, the mean of the nuclear distribution moved further toward the basal surface in treated retinas, and the concentration difference between the apical and basal surfaces diminished (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Described as experimental result and shown in Figures 4B, 4C, 4D

claim: In control retinas, the mean of the nuclear distribution moved toward the apical surface.
source: In contrast, in control retinas the mean of the nuclear distribution moved toward the apical surface (Figure 4A,C) as the gradient continued to build up.
evidence: Described as experimental result and shown in Figures 4A and 4C

claim: A lattice-gas based diffusion model is suitable to describe time evolution of the nuclear concentration profile during IKNM over several hours of early development.
source: These results show that a lattice-gas based diffusion model is indeed suitable to describe time evolution of the nuclear concentration profile of the zebrafish retina during IKNM over several hours of early development.

claim: Nuclear movements in IKNM cannot be due to thermal diffusion but must be actively driven.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the nuclear movements in IKNM cannot be due to thermal diffusion, but must be actively driven, for example through cytoskeletal transport.
evidence: Concluded from comparison of theoretical and experimental diffusion constants

claim: Forces underlying nuclear movement are estimated to be in the range of 1–50 nN.
source: As most molecular processes of cytoskeletal components have characteristic time scales of 10 ms to 1 s, we obtain forces in the range of 1–50 nN.
evidence: Calculated from diffusion constant and friction coefficient

claim: The estimated forces are compatible with cytoskeletal transport by multiple molecular motors or polymerization of cytoskeletal components.
source: This result is compatible with cytoskeletal transport under the assumption that the nucleus is transported either by multiple molecular motors at once, since each molecular motor protein typically exerts forces on the order of several pN, or through typical forces arising from polymerization of cytoskeletal components, which are in the same range (Peskin et al., 1993; Footer et al., 2007).
evidence: Comparison with known forces from cited literature

claim: IKNM cannot be understood as a single-cell phenomenon and requires explicitly taking surrounding nuclei into account.
source: First, they lend further support to the notion raised above that IKNM cannot be understood as a single-cell phenomenon. Instead, we can only interpret quantities such as MSD curves of nuclei undergoing IKNM correctly if we explicitly take the surrounding nuclei into account, even if there seems to be no direct energy transfer between nuclei, as shown from our experimental work (Figure 3).
evidence: Concluded from simulation results and experimental observations

claim: Cells are sensitive to the local nuclear concentration.
source: As the experimental MSD curve only agrees with the model that assumes a concentration-dependent stochastic force, among those considered, the results indicate that cells are, in some manner, sensitive to the local nuclear concentration.

claim: At high nuclear concentrations, cells may recruit more molecular motors to transport nuclei away from the apical surface faster.
source: At high nuclear concentrations (i.e. when nuclei are packed close to the maximum possible packing density), as is the case closest to the apical surface of the retinal tissue, cells may recruit more molecular motors to transport nuclei away from this surface faster, leading to the concentration dependence of the stochastic force.

claim: In high temperature (HT) conditions at 32°C, the average cell cycle length is 205.5 min.
source: We could directly measure the change in average cell cycle length from experimental data and found that in HT, it is 205.5 min, while in LT, it is a much larger 532.78 min.

claim: In low temperature (LT) conditions at 25°C, the average cell cycle length is 532.78 min.
source: We could directly measure the change in average cell cycle length from experimental data and found that in HT, it is 205.5 min, while in LT, it is a much larger 532.78 min.

claim: Incubation temperature influences IKNM directly by altering the mobility of nuclei.
source: These results indicate, that aside from its effect on cell cycle length, incubation temperature is likely to influence IKNM directly by altering the mobility of nuclei, here represented by the effective diffusion constant D.

claim: High-density nuclear trajectories can be used to tease apart possible physical processes behind stochastic nuclear movement during IKNM.
source: In this work, we have shown that high-density nuclear trajectories can be used to tease apart the possible physical processes behind the apparently stochastic movement of nuclei during interkinetic nuclear migration.

claim: A nuclear concentration gradient exists from the apical to the basal side of the tissue.
source: We confirmed the presence of a nuclear concentration gradient by calculating the nuclear concentration along the apicobasal dimension within the retinal tissue at various time points.

claim: The nuclear distribution flattened when cell division was inhibited with HU-AC treatment.
source: While we observed the build-up of the nuclear concentration gradient over time in the control retina, the nuclear distribution flattened when cell division was inhibited with HU-AC treatment.

claim: Only a small fraction of the apical tissue surface is occupied by mitotic cells at any given time.
source: Recent work indicates that only a small fraction of the apical tissue surface is occupied by mitotic cells at any given time (Matejčić et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Matejčić et al., 2018

claim: The nonlinear extension of the model incorporates a maximum possible nuclear concentration.
source: These phenomenological similarities between IKNM and diffusion suggested a model that includes two key features: firstly, it focuses on the crowding of nuclei at the apical surface of the tissue, here included as the apical boundary condition. Secondly, in the nonlinear extension of the model, it incorporates a maximum possible nuclear concentration.

claim: Both hindering and nonequilibrium driving forces have to be included to explain nuclear mobility.
source: Instead, it appears that both hindering and nonequilibrium driving forces have to be included, where nuclear mobility can be slowed-down due to the presence of the membrane and cytosolic composition and sped-up through active transport.

claim: MSD curves obtained in the presence of crowding are essentially linear, even though the underlying dynamics are nonlinear.
source: Importantly, the MSD curves obtained in the presence of crowding are essentially linear, even though the underlying dynamics are definitely nonlinear.

claim: The linearity of an MSD is not particularly probative of the underlying diffusive dynamics.
source: This illustrates clearly the fact that the linearity of an MSD is not, by itself, particularly probative of the underlying diffusive dynamics.

claim: Inanimate microbeads migrate much like nuclei during IKNM in the mouse cerebral cortex.
source: The fact that inanimate microbeads migrate much like nuclei during IKNM in the mouse cerebral cortex (Kosodo et al., 2011) suggests that active, unidirectional intracellular transport mechanisms are not directly responsible for these stochastic movements.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kosodo et al., 2011

claim: A passive diffusive process that takes steric interactions into account produces an excellent representation of nuclear distribution time evolution.
source: Instead, we show that a passive diffusive process which takes steric interactions between nuclei into account produces an excellent representation of the time evolution of the actual nuclear distribution within the retinal tissue during early development.

claim: Nuclei are moved by cytoskeletal transport throughout the entirety of the cell cycle.
source: The results of these microscopic considerations strongly suggest that nuclei are moved by means of cytoskeletal transport throughout the entirety of the cell cycle.

claim: Cytoskeletal transport during basal IKNM is highly stochastic, not unidirectional.
source: However, this transport appears not to be unidirectional but highly stochastic during basal IKNM.
evidence: Concluded from modeling and experimental results

claim: The stochastic forcing of nuclei is concentration-dependent.
source: Finally, an extension of the single nuclei equations to high concentrations and the results of stochastic simulations of nuclear trajectories suggest that the stochastic forcing of nuclei itself is concentration-dependent.

claim: The speed and dynamic properties of both microtubule and actomyosin systems are temperature dependent.
source: The fact that the speed and dynamic properties of both the microtubule and actomyosin systems are temperature dependent may explain the changes in the diffusion constant that we see as a function of temperature (Hartshorne et al., 1972; Hong et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hartshorne et al., 1972 and Hong et al., 2016

claim: A microtubule cage was observed around RPC nuclei.
source: For example, a microtubule cage was observed around RPC nuclei (Norden et al., 2009) and myosin was also shown to surround these nuclei (Leung et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Norden et al., 2009 and Leung et al., 2011

claim: Disruption of dynactin-1 functionality leads to more basal positioning of nuclei and occasional bursts of basal movement.
source: Disruption of a microtubule motor (dynactin-1) functionality either by mutation (Del Bene et al., 2008) or introduction of a dominant negative allele (Norden et al., 2009) leads to a more basal positioning of nuclei and occasional bursts of basal movement.
evidence: Supported by citations to Del Bene et al., 2008 and Norden et al., 2009

claim: In G2, a concentration of myosin at the basal side of the nucleus leads to rapid apical migration.
source: Finally, in G2 a concentration of myosin at the basal side of the nucleus leads to its rapid apical migration (Leung et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leung et al., 2011

claim: The G2 phase accounts for about 8% of the cell cycle in RPCs.
source: Nonetheless, despite the large displacement during rapid apical migration at G2, this phase only accounts for about 8% of the cell cycle in RPCs (Leung et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leung et al., 2011

claim: The calculated diffusion constant is in good agreement with those previously reported for individual nuclei.
source: Therefore, the good agreement of our calculated diffusion constant with those previously reported in the literature for individual nuclei (Leung et al., 2011) suggests that the proposed model describes tissue-wide IKNM quite well.

claim: Nuclear arrangements and IKNM have been implicated in stochastic cell fate decision making during differentiation.
source: This distribution has been implicated in stochastic cell fate decision making of progenitor cells during differentiation (Clark et al., 2012; Baye and Link, 2007; Hiscock et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clark et al., 2012, Baye and Link, 2007, and Hiscock et al., 2018

claim: A signaling gradient such as Notch may exist across the retina with location-dependent exposure important for decision-making.
source: Our observations would fit with previous suggestions that a signalling gradient, such as Notch, exists across the retina and location-dependent exposure to it is important for downstream decision-making (Murciano et al., 2002; Del Bene et al., 2008; Hiscock et al., 2018; Aggarwal et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Murciano et al., 2002, Del Bene et al., 2008, Hiscock et al., 2018, and Aggarwal et al., 2016

claim: All animal work was approved by the Local Ethical Review Committee of the University of Cambridge and performed under Home Office project license PL80/2198.
source: All animal works were approved by Local Ethical Review Committee of the University of Cambridge and performed in accordance with a Home Office project license PL80/2198.

claim: Zebrafish were maintained and bred at 26.5°C.
source: All zebrafish were maintained and bred at 26.5 °C.

claim: Embryos were incubated at 28.5°C before imaging sessions.
source: All embryos were incubated at 28.5 °C before imaging sessions.

claim: 0.003% phenylthiourea (PTU) was added to the medium at 10 hpf to stop pigmentation in the eye.
source: At 10 hr post-fertilization (hpf), 0.003% phenylthiourea (PTU) (sigma) was added to the medium to stop pigmentation in the eye.

claim: Double transgenic embryos Tg(bactin2:H2B-GFP::ptf1a:DsRed) were used for lightsheet microscopy.
source: Double transgenic embryos, Tg(bactin2:H2B-GFP::ptf1a:DsRed) were dechorionated at 24 hpf and screened positive for the fluorescent transgenic markers prior to the imaging experiment.

claim: Embryos were embedded in 0.4% low gelling temperature agarose for lightsheet imaging.
source: The embryo selected for imaging was then embedded in 0.4% low gelling temperature agarose (Type VII, Sigma-Aldrich) prepared in the imaging buffer (0.3x Daniau's solution with 0.2% tricaine and 0.003% PTU [Godinho, 2011]) within an FEP tube with 25 µm thick walls (Zeus), with an eye facing the camera and the illumination light shedding from the ventral side.

claim: A perfusion system was used to maintain a constant temperature of 28.5°C at the specimen location during lightsheet imaging.
source: To ensure normal development, a perfusion system was used to pump warm water into the specimen chamber, maintaining a constant temperature of 28.5 ºC at the location of the specimen.

claim: Time-lapse recording was performed using a SiMView light-sheet microscope with one illumination and one detection arm.
source: Time-lapse recording of retinal development was performed using a SiMView light-sheet microscope (Tomer et al., 2012) with one illumination and one detection arm.

claim: GFP was excited with 488 nm laser and detected through a 525/50 nm band pass filter.
source: GFP was excited with scanned light sheets using a 488 nm laser, and detected through a 525/50 nm band pass detection filter (Semrock).

claim: Image stacks were acquired with confocal slit detection with 10 ms exposure time per frame.
source: Image stacks were acquired with confocal slit detection (Baumgart and Kubitscheck, 2012) with exposure time of 10 ms per frame, and the sample was moved in 0.812 µm steps along the axial direction.

claim: Two 330 × 330 × 250 µm³ image stacks with 40 µm horizontal offset were acquired at each time point.
source: For each time point, two 330 × 330 × 250 µm3 image stacks with a 40 µm horizontal offset were acquired to ensure the coverage of the entire retina.

claim: Images were acquired every 2 min from 30 hpf to 72 hpf for lightsheet microscopy.
source: The images were acquired every 2 min from 30 hpf to 72 hpf.

claim: A TriM Scope II 2-photon microscope was used for the repetition data set and other conditions.
source: Images for the repetition data set and all other conditions were obtained using a TriM Scope II 2-photon microscope (LaVision BioTec).

claim: Embryos were embedded in 0.9% UltraPure low melting point agarose for two-photon microscopy.
source: An embryo was then embedded in 0.9% UltraPure low melting point agarose (Invitrogen) prepared in E3 medium containing 0.003% PTU and 0.2% tricaine.

claim: For cell cycle arrest experiments, hydroxyurea and aphidicolin were added to final concentrations of 20 mM and 150 µM, respectively.
source: For the experiment involving cell cycle arrest, hydroxyurea and aphidicolin (Abcam) were added to the incubation solution right before imaging, to a final concentration of 20 mM and 150 µM, respectively.

claim: Green fluorescence was excited using an Insight DeepSee laser at 927 nm for two-photon microscopy.
source: Green fluorescence was excited using an Insight DeepSee laser (Spectra-Physics) at 927 nm.

claim: Image stacks with 1 μm step size were acquired with 1.35 ms exposure time per line averaged over two scans for two-photon microscopy.
source: Image stacks with step size of 1 μm were acquired with exposure time of 1.35 ms per line averaged over two scans.

claim: Images were recorded every 2 min for 10–15 hrs starting at 26–28 hpf for two-photon microscopy.
source: The images were recorded every 2 min for 10–15 hrs starting at 26–28 hpf.

claim: Fits with a wide range of numbers of modes resulted in the same optimal D-values.
source: Fits with a wide range of numbers of modes were found to result in the same optimal D-values.

claim: The exact choice of exclusion width was found not to influence the fitting result for the nonlinear model.
source: The exact choice of exclusion width was found not to influence the fitting result for the nonlinear model.

claim: Time discretization of stochastic differential equations was achieved via the Euler-Maruyama method.
source: Time discretization of the stochastic differential equations was achieved via the Euler-Maruyama method.

claim: Simulations were performed using 0.2 min time steps.
source: Simulations were performed using 0.2 min time steps and were checked against those with smaller time steps to ensure that this choice was sufficiently small.

claim: 40 nuclei were simulated in each run with birth times matching experimental data.
source: In each run of a simulation, 40 nuclei were simulated and their birth times within the simulation were chosen to be the same birth times as those obtained from the nuclei within the experiments.

claim: Each nucleus was simulated for a total of 150 min.
source: Each nucleus was simulated for a total of 150 min, corresponding to the chosen experimental data.

claim: The same simulation was repeated 2500 times for each model to obtain the range of MSD curves.
source: For each model, the same simulation was repeated 2500 times to obtain the range of distributions of the resulting mean squared displacement curves.

claim: Two-sided unequal variances t-tests (Welch's t-test) were performed to determine whether samples differ significantly.
source: Two sided tests, specifically unequal variances t-test, also known as Welch's t-test, (Precht and Kraft, 2015), were performed in order to determine whether samples differ significantly from each other.

claim: There is no significant difference between D-values obtained from the two normal condition data sets.
source: Based on these values, two-sided t-tests (see Materials and methods) confirmed that there is no significant difference between the D-values obtained from the two normal condition data sets.
